questions.title: How exactly does the partition function cancel when reparameterizing reward in Eq. (4)?
questions.question_body:
In the paper, they start from the optimal policy representation

\(\pi_r(y\mid x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)}\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp\left(\frac{1}{\beta}r(x,y)\right)\)

and then log-transform to get Eq. (4):

\(r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_r(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)} + \beta \log Z(x).\)

They then say that substituting this into the Bradley–Terry model cancels the partition function. Could someone show the algebraic steps that prove the cancellation explicitly, i.e., starting from

\(p^*(y_1\succ y_2\mid x)=\sigma(r^*(x,y_1)-r^*(x,y_2))\)

and substituting Eq. (4) to get Eq. (6)? I get confused about where the \(\beta\log Z(x)\) term goes.

questions.title: Why is the reparameterization \(r(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}\) not restrictive? What reward functions does it exclude?
questions.question_body:
The authors claim in Theorem 1 that every reward class consistent with Plackett–Luce / Bradley–Terry can be represented as

\(r(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}\)

up to adding a function of \(x\). I find this surprising: aren't there reward functions that cannot be written as the log-ratio of two policies (times \(\beta\))? Intuitively, what assumptions are required for this to hold, and can you give a counterexample if any assumption is violated?

questions.title: What is the role of the equivalence class of reward functions and why can we ignore additive functions of \(x\)?
questions.question_body: The paper defines two reward functions as equivalent if they differ by a function that depends only on \(x\). Why does the Plackett–Luce / Bradley–Terry preference model make these additive \(x\)-dependent offsets unobservable? How does this justify learning only the reward up to an additive function of \(x\)?

questions.title: How is the reference policy \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) chosen in practice and how sensitive is DPO to its mis-specification?
questions.question_body: DPO requires a reference policy \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\), often the SFT model. The authors also propose fitting \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) by maximizing likelihood on the preferred completions when an SFT is unavailable. But how sensitive is DPO to a poorly matched \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\)? If \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) is far from the true sampling policy used to collect preferences, will DPO produce biased or unstable results?

questions.title: In Eq. (7) the DPO loss uses \(\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}\). Are these sequence-level probabilities or product of token-level probabilities?
questions.question_body: When implementing DPO with autoregressive LMs, do we compute \(\pi_\theta(y\mid x)\) as the full sequence probability (product of per-token probabilities) and take the log, or do we work token-by-token? Are there numerical/stability issues computing full sequence probabilities for long outputs? The paper also mentions sequence-level KL; how is that computed in practice?

questions.title: Derivation of the DPO gradient: where does the weighting term \(\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w))\) come from?
questions.question_body:
In the paper the gradient of the DPO loss is given as

\(-\beta \mathbb{E}[\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w)) (\nabla_\theta\log\pi(y_w|x)-\nabla_\theta\log\pi(y_l|x))]\).

I understand the sign and the log-derivative terms, but I'd like a step-by-step derivation from the cross-entropy loss in Eq. (7) that yields the logistic-sigma weight. Is that just differentiation of \(\log\sigma(\Delta)\) with \(\Delta=\beta(\hat r(y_w)-\hat r(y_l))\)?

questions.title: Why does omitting the logistic weight lead to model degeneration, and what kind of degeneration occurs?
questions.question_body: The authors note that a naive objective that simply increases the probability ratio of preferred over dispreferred responses without the \(\sigma(\cdot)\) weight can make the LM 'degenerate'. What exactly is the degeneration observed (mode collapse, repeated tokens, training instability?), and can you provide an intuition why the weight prevents this?

questions.title: Can DPO be extended to rankings over more than two responses (full Plackett–Luce), and how would the loss change?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions Plackett–Luce models and that the derivation extends beyond Bradley–Terry. If we have ranked lists or top-k preferences instead of pairwise comparisons, how do we write the DPO loss? Does the partition-function cancellation still occur in those cases?

questions.title: Is DPO just performing maximum likelihood under a Bradley–Terry model with a particular parameterization? If so, how is it different from directly fitting the reward's logistic regression?
questions.question_body: I see that DPO's loss in Eq. (7) is a cross-entropy on the pairwise labels, but with inputs equal to \(\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta}{\pi_{\text{ref}}}\). How is this conceptually different from fitting a reward model \(r_\phi\) with the same cross-entropy and then doing RL to get the policy? Is DPO just moving the optimization variable from reward to policy to avoid an RL stage?

questions.title: How does DPO compare to Unlikelihood training mathematically, and why does Unlikelihood underperform in experiments?
questions.question_body: Unlikelihood minimizes probability of dispreferred completions and increases preferred ones (with coefficient \(\alpha\)). Can you show the mathematical difference between Unlikelihood and DPO objectives? Why would DPO be expected to be more stable or effective?

questions.title: What exactly is the constrained objective that DPO optimizes equivalently to RLHF, and how do we know DPO finds the optimum?
questions.question_body:
The RLHF objective is

\(\max_\pi \mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi}[r(x,y)] - \beta D_{\text{KL}}[\pi \| \pi_{\text{ref}}]\).

DPO is derived by parameterizing the optimal policy and fitting it via preferences. Under what conditions can we guarantee that minimizing the DPO loss recovers the policy that maximizes the RLHF objective? Is there a consistency theorem or is it dependent on model capacity and data?

questions.title: How should one choose the temperature-like hyperparameter \(\beta\) in practice?
questions.question_body: The algorithm uses \(\beta\) as the KL penalty scale. The experiments use a small sweep of values (e.g., \{0.05,0.1,1,5\}). Is there a principled way to pick \(\beta\) based on desired KL budget or examples, or should it be tuned empirically? What are the qualitative effects of larger vs smaller \(\beta\)?

questions.title: In Eq. (7) the logistic argument is scaled by \(\beta\). Is the sign convention consistent when \(\beta\) is positive? Could negative \(\beta\) make sense?
questions.question_body: The loss uses \(\sigma(\beta(\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w)} - \log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l)}))\). The paper treats \(\beta>0\). What if someone tries to set \(\beta<0\) (i.e., reward encourages moving away from \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\))? Is that invalid, unstable, or meaningful? Is there an interpretation of \(\beta\) as an inverse temperature vs regularization coefficient?

questions.title: How are gradients computed in minibatches: do we backprop through both numerator and denominator policies when computing log-ratios?
questions.question_body: In training DPO with SGD, each loss term contains \(\log\pi_\theta(y\mid x) - \log\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\). The latter is a constant if \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) is fixed, but sometimes \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) could be a trained network. Do we ever update \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) jointly? If not, we can treat \(\log\pi_{\text{ref}}\) as a constant. If yes, how is that handled to avoid trivial solutions?

questions.title: Why does DPO avoid needing a baseline/value function, and what was the instability baseline was supposed to address in PPO?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that the normalization term in the actor-critic objective corresponds to the soft value function and that actor-critic approaches need to learn that baseline, causing instability. Why does DPO avoid learning that baseline entirely? Is it because the reparameterization implicitly sets the value baseline to make the partition function 1 (Eq. 11)?

questions.title: How does DPO handle off-policy preference data collected from a different policy than \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\)?
questions.question_body: Preference datasets are sometimes collected using different sampling policies. The paper recommends initializing \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) by maximizing likelihood of preferred completions if the true SFT is unavailable. But if the data were collected from a significantly different policy, would the log-ratio term be miscalibrated? Does DPO require importance weighting when reusing arbitrary offline preference datasets?

questions.title: What is the computational cost of DPO compared to PPO during training and at inference?
questions.question_body: The paper claims DPO is computationally lightweight because it avoids sampling during training and complex RL loops. Could you provide an outline of the cost components (forward/backward passes per dataset example) for DPO vs PPO, and also comment on inference cost differences (e.g., Best-of-N requires N samples at inference)?

questions.title: How are multiple tokens and sequence lengths handled when computing the sequence-level KL in the experiments?
questions.question_body:
The experiments report sequence-level KL, defined as sum of per-timestep KL. Is the KL computed as

\(\text{KL}(\pi\|\pi_{\text{ref}}) = \sum_{t} \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\text{KL}(\pi(\cdot|x,y_{<t})\|\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot|x,y_{<t}))]\)

or as the KL on full sequence distributions? Practically, what approximation is used and how does it affect comparisons?

questions.title: Why does DPO tend to be more robust to sampling temperature than PPO in experiments?
questions.question_body: The TL;DR results show DPO's performance is less sensitive to sampling temperature than PPO. Is there an intuitive / theoretical reason why DPO-trained policies generate better quality across temperatures? Does the implicit reward parameterization produce different entropy properties in the trained policy?

questions.title: Can DPO learn to increase diversity or does it encourage mode-seeking behavior?
questions.question_body: Because DPO increases probability of preferred outputs but constrains KL to a reference policy, does it encourage preserving the entropy/diversity of the reference? Are there failure modes where DPO collapses to fewer modes, and if so how can we detect/mitigate them?

questions.title: Does DPO provide any guarantees about converging to a von Neumann winner in contextual dueling bandit terminology?
questions.question_body: The related work mentions von Neumann winners in contextual dueling bandits. Given a fixed offline set of pairwise preferences, can DPO be interpreted as finding a policy that maximizes expected win-rate (i.e., a von Neumann winner) or is it explicitly optimizing the KL-constrained reward objective instead? How do these perspectives relate?

questions.title: How does DPO generalize under distribution shift compared to PPO: why might it do better on CNN/DM after training on Reddit TL;DR?
questions.question_body: The paper shows DPO outperforms PPO when both trained on Reddit TL;DR but evaluated on CNN/DailyMail. What could explain DPO's better generalization? Is it due to avoiding RL sampling noise, or because DPO optimizes a parametric policy directly so the learned policy aligns better with training data distribution?

questions.title: Is there any risk of reward hacking or adversarial behavior when using DPO because it bypasses explicit reward modeling?
questions.question_body: By folding reward implicitly into the policy via the log-ratio parameterization, do we lose transparency into what the learned reward is? Could this hide perverse incentives or reward hacking behavior that would be easier to inspect when training an explicit reward model?

questions.title: How would you implement DPO with batched training data when the preference pairs share the same prompt but different response lengths?
questions.question_body: In practice, prompts may appear multiple times with different candidate responses of varying lengths. When forming minibatches and computing \(\log\pi(y|x)\) for each candidate, is it acceptable to truncate/pad sequences? Are there best practices for batching efficiency and gradient estimation when responses have variable lengths?

questions.title: Can you use DPO iteratively to collect more data via self-labeling (i.e., generate samples from the current policy and relabel)? What are the caveats?
questions.question_body: The Discussion mentions self-labeling and using unlabeled prompts. If I sample new completions from the current DPO policy and label them (with humans or a rubric), can I safely continue training with DPO? Could this lead to distributional drift or compounding biases, and are there recommended safeguards?

questions.title: How would you recover or interpret the implicit reward \(\hat r_\theta(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}\) numerically for inspection or debugging?
questions.question_body: If I want to examine which outputs are assigned high implicit reward by the DPO-trained policy, what's the correct way to compute and normalize \(\hat r_\theta\) across different prompts so that values are comparable? Should one subtract an \(x\)-dependent baseline to make rewards comparable across prompts?

questions.title: How does DPO handle ties or noisy human labels where preferences are inconsistent?
questions.question_body: Human annotators may disagree or provide stochastic labels; Bradley–Terry models account for stochasticity, but in DPO we directly optimize policy likelihood ratios. Does DPO naturally deal with noisy labels (e.g. annotator A prefers y1, annotator B prefers y2) or do we need to adjust loss weighting or regularization to avoid overfitting noise?

questions.title: Is there any connection between DPO and inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) or maximum entropy IRL?
questions.question_body: DPO maps preferences to a policy by using a log-ratio parameterization reminiscent of energy-based or maximum-entropy formulations. Can we view DPO as performing a form of IRL where the reward is recovered implicitly from a policy, and if so, how does it relate to maximum-entropy IRL or apprenticeship learning frameworks?
